note: Hand-written per-screen design-parity inventory. Every row below is written by hand, not discovered by scanning app/src/ui -- a screen that disappeared from the app would disappear from an auto-generated list too, which defeats the point of this file. The route set is taken from app/src/ui/routes.ts (13 destinations: 4 primary + 9 tools); that file is the single source of truth for what screens this application has.
realAppEntryPoint: app/main.js via electron.exe app --user-data-dir=<fresh temp dir> (no query-param routing exists in app/src/ui -- every real-app route below is reached by clicking the nav-rail item with the stated Material Symbols ligature name, at coordinates recorded per screen; the Tools section below the fold is reached by clicking an inert nav-rail gutter pixel to focus the scrollable list, then sending the End key)
capturedAtDate: second evidence pass -- re-captured after the settings placeholder, Tools drawer duplication, and regex/builder translation fixes landed on main

determinismNotes: The startup dim-sum surprise (app/src/ui/dim-sum-surprise.tsx) fires on ~1/10 launches; every app-side capture below was taken from a launch where it did not fire. A capture whose screenshot shows the surprise overlay must be discarded and re-captured from a fresh launch, never accepted as-is.

Each app-side launch uses a fresh --user-data-dir under a temp directory so package-manager availability probing and any persisted state cannot vary between runs, and so requestSingleInstanceLock() cannot reject the launch against a sibling worktree's live instance sharing the default userData path.

The real app queries live winget/scoop/etc. on the host machine, so the *content* of the Updates, Discover, Installed and Bundles lists is real, host-specific package data, not the reference's fixture data. This is expected and is not a parity defect: the row's MD3 audit and diff record judge chrome, layout and component anatomy, not list contents. The diff percentage is reported honestly and reflects this for exactly those rows.

The Authenticator, Operation history and Logs screens likewise show the reference's curated sample data against the real app's genuinely empty/session-scoped state (no TOTP secrets registered, no operations run yet in this session). Recorded as a reviewed content deviation per row, not a defect.

diffMethodology.alignment: Both captures are aligned on the app's brand-logo icon (a small saturated dark-blue square in the top app bar) before diffing, because the reference is captured through a real Edge app-mode window while the real app is a frameless Electron window with a different, slightly shorter custom title bar. The discovered offset (dx=-3, dy=-31 px) is identical across every screen, which is the signature of a genuine constant chrome-height difference rather than per-screen noise. See script/design-parity/diff.mjs for the full method and its fallback.
diffMethodology.levelNormalization: The reference capture renders with a uniform, exactly-reproducible RGB(102,102,102) background -- confirmed by direct pixel sampling and by a freshly relaunched, never-interacted-with capture showing the identical value -- which is precisely white (255) scaled by 0.4, i.e. a 60%-opacity black scrim. This is not present in the real app's identically-captured output and reproduces on every reference screen, so it is treated as a capture-environment artifact of the reference tool (most likely the design canvas dimming in response to the Page Visibility API reporting the window as backgrounded on a non-interactive Win32 desktop station), not a property of the design or the port. Both images are auto-levelled to their own 95th-percentile brightness before diffing to correct it; the discovered white points are recorded per screen in diff-report.json so the correction is inspectable rather than hidden.
diffMethodology.readingTheNumbers: A GOOD value for a chrome/structure-only screen (no live host data) is under ~5%: residual difference from anti-aliasing, font hinting, and small deliberate deviations. A screen whose content is genuinely different data (Updates, Discover, Installed, Bundles, Authenticator, Operation history: reference fixture vs real host/session state) will read higher -- roughly 8-20% observed -- and that is expected, not a failure; the side-by-side image is the actual evidence for those rows, not the number alone. A value approaching 50%+ on a screen that should hold static content is the number that means something is actually wrong.

The real app's content (unsigned-artifact disclosure, data-folder path, package-manager driver note) is real and useful, but it does not correspond 1:1 to any single reference tab.
